summary: Rotation Compass is a free web tool that helps a farmer compare crop rotations for one field using NASA Earth data. The farmer clicks the field on a map and enters the current four-year rotation, soil type, slope, irrigation and priorities (saving water, soil health or income). The tool then downloads 25 years of NASA POWER monthly data for that point: rainfall, temperature, solar radiation and root-zone soil wetness. From these it calculates evaporation demand and the water deficit month by month, and compares the current rotation with two alternatives: one that brings in a legume and cover crops, and one built around drought-tolerant crops. Each option gets scores for water fit, soil health, erosion protection, pest break and income, a month-by-month field calendar, and a plain-language note on why it was suggested, which numbers support it and what a local agronomist should check. The tool was made with southern Ukraine in mind, where sunflower-heavy rotations meet summers that NASA data shows getting hotter and drier.
details:
What it does and how it works

Rotation Compass runs in any browser, including a phone, and needs no login or installation. The farmer chooses a field on a map, describes the current rotation and the farm, and presses one button. The page requests monthly data for 2001–2025 from the NASA POWER API for that point and builds a climate profile: yearly rainfall, the April–September water balance, July root-zone soil wetness, July heat, April frost days, August–September rain and 25-year trends. Reference evapotranspiration is estimated with the Hargreaves–Samani equation from POWER temperature and top-of-atmosphere radiation.

Three rotations are compared. The first is the farmer's own. The second keeps it but replaces the weakest link (a crop that returns too often or has the poorest water fit) with a legume chosen for the local climate (pea, chickpea or soybean) and fills long bare periods with a cover crop or stubble. The third is built for the climate profile of the point; for a dry point it uses chickpea, winter barley and sorghum. Each rotation is scored on water fit, soil health, erosion protection, pest and disease break and income potential, and the farmer's priorities set the weights. A field calendar shows, month by month over four years, when the soil is covered and how much rain falls on bare ground.

Example: for a point in Kherson region, NASA POWER gives 441 mm of rain a year, a 591 mm water deficit from April to September and summers warming by about 0.9 °C per decade. The common wheat–sunflower–maize–sunflower rotation leaves the soil bare 20 months out of 48 and scores 52 out of 100. The drought-oriented option scores 76 with no bare months, at the cost of lower income potential.

Benefits and intended impact

Every suggestion comes with its reasons, the NASA numbers behind it and a list of things to check locally: seed inoculant for legumes, herbicide carry-over, buyers for chickpea or sorghum, autumn rain for cover crops. The tool helps a farmer prepare questions for an agronomist; the final choice stays with the farmer. Many farms in southern Ukraine lost irrigation after the Kakhovka dam was destroyed in 2023 and now need rotations that work on rain alone.

Tools and technologies

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one static page hosted on GitHub Pages; Leaflet for the map with OpenStreetMap tiles; Chart.js for charts; the NASA POWER API; NASA GIBS map tiles (MODIS Terra NDVI, MODIS true colour, SMAP Level-4 root-zone soil moisture). The interface is in English and Ukrainian, and every analysis can be shared as a link. Code: https://github.com/KirillUltra/rotation-compass

Creativity and factors considered

The field calendar turns rotation advice into a picture a farmer can read in seconds. Water fit accounts for sunflower and maize drying out the subsoil for the next crop in dry areas. The page states its limits openly: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km wide, soil and slope come from the user, and income uses relative crop values rather than current prices.

Use of AI

The code and texts were written with the help of Claude (Anthropic), an AI assistant, and reviewed by the author. All rules and data sources are visible in the page source and the README.
